lead: Getting one thing wrong doesn't mean you're no good as a person.
when: When one slip makes you want to give up on everything, or an argument in a relationship turns into "you always...", use it to slow down.
body:
"Either it's perfect or it's pointless." "If you don't back me, you don't care about me." "I broke my diet today, so the whole week is ruined." Thoughts like these, which leave only two extremes, are black-and-white thinking. They let you reach a conclusion fast, but throw away all the useful information in between.

In cognitive psychology, this is usually called "all-or-nothing thinking": seeing a complex situation as two mutually exclusive extremes and ignoring differences of degree and the possibilities in between.

Most of life looks more like this: some parts are good and some still need work; you didn't manage it this time, but you did before. Describing things more specifically isn't just consoling yourself; it leaves room for the next step. You don't have to declare your whole self a winner or a loser before you can deal with one small problem.

Many real-life assessments are more like a scale than two on-off switches. "I didn't do well this time" may just mean one step needs fixing; it doesn't jump straight to "I'm completely hopeless." Find where you are on the scale first, then decide which way to adjust.
example:
You plan to read twenty pages a day. You keep it up for four days, then on day five you're too busy and skip it, and immediately think, "I knew I couldn't stick with it." That verdict wipes out four days of effort and makes starting again on day six even harder.

Try putting it another way: "I read on four days this week. Twenty pages is too much when I'm busy, so next time my minimum is two pages." You're not pretending a missed day doesn't matter, and you're not throwing the whole thing away because of one missed day. That makes the plan easier to keep going.
extra: A conflict in a relationship doesn't mean all the past caring was fake, but past caring doesn't mean the current problem can be ignored either. Letting both things be true at once is usually closer to reality.
steps: Notice words like "always," "never," "totally," and "not even once" in what you say.
Find one example, however small, that doesn't fully fit the conclusion.
Swap a label for your whole self with a specific situation and a next step, like "I need to practice my opening."
caution: Some things really do need a clear yes or no, like whether you met a deadline. This model isn't about making every rule fuzzy; it's about not inflating one result into a verdict on your whole life.
exercise: Write down an absolute judgment that's been hurting you lately. Delete "always," "never," and "completely," add the specific time and event, then read it again.
brief: Polarized versus continuous: above, a stick figure is stuck between an all-black block and an all-white block, with only two endpoints; below, a long bar is divided into steps from white to dark gray with many possible stopping places in between, and a stick figure looks at a specific position.
diagramCaption: Between the two extremes, there are usually many distinct positions.
